items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A vertical section through a soil showing its horizons from the surface to the parent rock"?
items.answer: soil profile
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of soil profile.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the A horizon and the B horizon.
items.answer: The A horizon (topsoil) is dark, mixed with humus, biologically active and loses material by eluviation; the B horizon (subsoil) is lighter, lower in organic matter and gains clay, iron and aluminium washed down from above.
items.markingKey: The A horizon (topsoil) is dark, mixed with humus, biologically active and loses material by eluviation; the B horizon (subsoil) is lighter, lower in organic matter and gains clay, iron and aluminium washed down from above. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why tropical rainforest soils are often thin and infertile.
items.answer: High rainfall leaches soluble nutrients; rapid decomposition and uptake mean nutrients are stored in biomass, not soil; deep weathering leaves iron- and aluminium-rich oxisols with little humus.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: High rainfall leaches soluble nutrients; rapid decomposition and uptake mean nutrients are stored in biomass, not soil; deep weathering leaves iron- and aluminium-rich oxisols with little humus. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Soil is just crushed rock." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Soil is a mixture of mineral particles, organic matter (humus), water, air and living organisms, and has structure and horizons formed by soil processes.
items.markingKey: Soil is a mixture of mineral particles, organic matter (humus), water, air and living organisms, and has structure and horizons formed by soil processes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe chernozems of the Ukrainian steppe and explain what it reveals about how climate and vegetation shape soil profiles.
items.answer: Deep, black soils up to 1 m thick formed under grassland, with high humus content (up to 10-15%). Grass roots die back each year adding organic matter, while moderate rainfall limits leaching, building one of the world's most fertile soils.
items.markingKey: Context (Deep, black soils up to 1 m thick formed under grassland, with high humus content (up to 10-15%).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Grass roots die back each year adding organic matter, while moderate rainfall limits leaching, building one of the world's most fertile soils. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how climate and vegetation shape soil profiles.

items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that soil should be managed as a non-renewable resource.
items.answer: On human timescales soil should be treated as effectively non-renewable, though its quality can be restored if not lost.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: formation rate ~1 t/ha/yr vs erosion up to 10-100 t/ha/yr; a third of soils are moderately or highly degraded (FAO 2015). Limitations / counter-points: soil organic matter and structure can be rebuilt with good management; some soils form faster (volcanic, alluvial). Conclusion: On human timescales soil should be treated as effectively non-renewable, though its quality can be restored if not lost. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "humus"?
options: The breakdown of rock in situ by physical, chemical and biological processes, producing the mineral fraction of soil
Dark, partially decomposed organic matter in soil that holds water and nutrients
The ability of a soil to supply nutrients, water and air to plants for growth
The accumulation of salts in soil, often caused by irrigation in hot climates where evaporation draws saline water to the surface
items.answer: Dark, partially decomposed organic matter in soil that holds water and nutrients
items.markingKey: B. "humus" is dark, partially decomposed organic matter in soil that holds water and nutrients.

items.stem: Outline why soils are described as a non-renewable resource.
items.answer: Soil forms extremely slowly (about 1 cm per 100-400 years), whereas erosion from poorly managed land can remove centimetres in a few years; lost soil cannot be replaced on human timescales.
items.markingKey: Soil forms extremely slowly (about 1 cm per 100-400 years), whereas erosion from poorly managed land can remove centimetres in a few years; lost soil cannot be replaced on human timescales. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Describe the soil profile of a podzol under a boreal coniferous forest.
items.answer: Acidic needle litter (O); thin dark A; grey, bleached E horizon from intense leaching of iron and humus; reddish-brown B horizon where iron and humus accumulate (iron pan); C horizon.
items.markingKey: Acidic needle litter (O); thin dark A; grey, bleached E horizon from intense leaching of iron and humus; reddish-brown B horizon where iron and humus accumulate (iron pan); C horizon.

items.answer: Texture sets the baseline, but management largely determines whether productivity is achieved and sustained.

items.stem: Explain why soil organic matter is important for fertility.
items.answer: It supplies nutrients as it decomposes, increases CEC and water retention, binds particles into stable crumbs, feeds soil organisms and buffers pH.

items.answer: Crumb structure creates pores for air and water, allows roots to penetrate and supports soil organisms; compaction or platy structure reduces infiltration, causes waterlogging and limits root growth.

items.stem: Soil loss from a vineyard on a hillside in the Douro valley, Portugal, bare soil between rows, is 5 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹. The soil bulk density is 1.4 t m⁻³ and the topsoil is 200 mm deep (1 mm of soil over 1 ha = 10 m³). (a) Calculate the depth of soil lost per year in mm. (b) Calculate how long the topsoil would last. (c) Contour ploughing and cover crops are expected to cut erosion by 90%. Calculate the new loss and evaluate whether this would be sustainable if soil forms at 1.0 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹.
items.answer: (a) 5 t ÷ 1.4 t m⁻³ = 3.6 m³ per ha = 0.36 mm per year (b) 200 / 0.36 ≈ 560 years (c) 0.5 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹; at or below the formation rate, so sustainable

items.answer: Farmers protect and prune sprouting tree stumps rather than clearing them; about 5 million ha have been re-greened since the 1980s, reducing wind erosion, adding organic matter and increasing yields.
items.markingKey: Farmers protect and prune sprouting tree stumps rather than clearing them; about 5 million ha have been re-greened since the 1980s, reducing wind erosion, adding organic matter and increasing yields.

items.stem: A 200 g soil sample from a vegetable plot in Nairobi contained sand 90 g, silt 80 g and clay 30 g. Simplified classification: clay ≥ 40%; sand ≥ 85%; silt ≥ 80%; loam if sand 23-52%, silt 28-50% and clay 7-27%; sandy loam if sand 52-85% and clay < 20%; otherwise clay loam. (a) Calculate the percentage composition and classify the soil. (b) Describe how this texture affects its suitability for agriculture. (c) Suggest one way to improve it.
items.answer: (a) sand 45%, silt 40%, clay 15% → loam (b) balanced drainage, water retention and nutrient-holding capacity - ideal for most crops (c) e.g. add organic matter (compost, manure) to improve structure, water retention and drainage; liming or drainage where needed.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 percentages, A1 loam. (b) R1 R1 properties linked to texture. (c) R1 valid improvement.

items.stem: Suggest three soil conservation strategies for a hillside farm in Nepal.
items.answer: Terracing; contour ploughing and grass strips; agroforestry; mulching and cover crops; avoiding cultivation of the steepest slopes; check dams in gullies.
items.markingKey: Terracing; contour ploughing and grass strips; agroforestry; mulching and cover crops; avoiding cultivation of the steepest slopes; check dams in gullies.

items.stem: "Soil conservation is more cost-effective than restoring degraded land." Discuss this statement with reference to named examples. [9]

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that soil should be managed as a non-renewable resource. [9]
items.answer: On human timescales soil should be treated as effectively non-renewable, though its quality can be restored if not lost.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "soil degradation"?
options: The decline in soil quality through erosion, loss of organic matter, salinisation, compaction, acidification, contamination or nutrient depletion
Ploughing across a slope following the contours, so furrows trap water and soil and reduce erosion
The breakdown of rock in situ by physical, chemical and biological processes, producing the mineral fraction of soil
Dark, partially decomposed organic matter in soil that holds water and nutrients
items.answer: The decline in soil quality through erosion, loss of organic matter, salinisation, compaction, acidification, contamination or nutrient depletion
items.markingKey: A. "soil degradation" is the decline in soil quality through erosion, loss of organic matter, salinisation, compaction, acidification, contamination or nutrient depletion.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "leaching".
items.answer: The removal of soluble minerals and nutrients from the upper soil horizons by water percolating downwards
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the removal of soluble minerals and nutrients from the upper soil horizons by water percolating downwards. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.answer: soil texture

items.stem: Outline how no-till (conservation) agriculture reduces soil degradation.
items.answer: Crops are sown directly into the residue of the previous crop; residues protect the surface from raindrop impact and wind, increase organic matter and soil biota, improve infiltration and reduce erosion and fuel use.
items.markingKey: Crops are sown directly into the residue of the previous crop; residues protect the surface from raindrop impact and wind, increase organic matter and soil biota, improve infiltration and reduce erosion and fuel use. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Outline how soil acts as a system.
items.answer: It has inputs (organic matter, precipitation, weathered parent material, energy), storages (organic matter, nutrients, water, air, organisms), transfers (leaching, translocation) and transformations (decomposition, weathering, humification), and outputs (uptake by plants, erosion, leaching, gases).

items.stem: A student claims: "Fertiliser alone can maintain soil fertility indefinitely." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Fertiliser supplies nutrients but does not maintain structure, organic matter or soil life; organic matter decline leads to erosion and lower yields.
items.markingKey: Fertiliser supplies nutrients but does not maintain structure, organic matter or soil life; organic matter decline leads to erosion and lower yields. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between acidification and salinisation.
items.answer: Salinisation is the build-up of salts, usually from irrigation in hot climates; acidification is a fall in soil pH from acid rain, ammonium fertilisers or conifer litter.
items.markingKey: Salinisation is the build-up of salts, usually from irrigation in hot climates; acidification is a fall in soil pH from acid rain, ammonium fertilisers or conifer litter. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why soils are described as a non-renewable resource.
items.answer: Soil forms extremely slowly (about 1 cm per 100-400 years), whereas erosion from poorly managed land can remove centimetres in a few years; lost soil cannot be replaced on human timescales.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Soil forms extremely slowly (about 1 cm per 100-400 years), whereas erosion from poorly managed land can remove centimetres in a few years; lost soil cannot be replaced on human timescales. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Compare sandy soils with clay soils.
items.answer: Sandy soils have large particles and pores, drain freely, warm quickly and are easily leached of nutrients; clay soils have tiny particles, hold water and nutrients well but drain poorly and compact easily.
items.markingKey: Sandy soils have large particles and pores, drain freely, warm quickly and are easily leached of nutrients; clay soils have tiny particles, hold water and nutrients well but drain poorly and compact easily. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: With reference to salinisation in the Murray-Darling Basin, Australia, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in salinisation as a form of soil degradation. [7]
items.answer: Clearing deep-rooted native vegetation and irrigation raised water tables, bringing salt to the surface and affecting millions of hectares. Rising groundwater carried salts into the root zone, making land unproductive. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: Soil loss from a soybean field in Mato Grosso, Brazil, after the first rains, is 30 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹. The soil bulk density is 1.4 t m⁻³ and the topsoil is 250 mm deep (1 mm of soil over 1 ha = 10 m³). (a) Calculate the depth of soil lost per year in mm. (b) Calculate how long the topsoil would last. (c) Contour ploughing and cover crops are expected to cut erosion by 90%. Calculate the new loss and evaluate whether this would be sustainable if soil forms at 0.5 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹.
items.answer: (a) 30 t ÷ 1.4 t m⁻³ = 21.4 m³ per ha = 2.14 mm per year (b) 250 / 2.14 ≈ 117 years (c) 3.0 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹; still above the formation rate, so not yet sustainable - further measures (terracing, agroforestry) are needed
